proof.criterion: A1 - an options edit keeps an option it does not change, node for node
proof.surface: the real dispatch CLI against a real Dispatch server in this pod (packages/dispatch/e2e/run-server.sh on Postgres 17 with pgvector, port 8779, agent token e2e-token)
proof.command: dispatch issue --project HEAD --title 'An options edit keeps an option it does not change' --spec-file - (an ask whose gRPC option holds bold, a link, a second paragraph and a sub-list); dispatch edit-ask --ask eb2487bc-f749-4685-8fc3-a6d4a89d05ac --option 'REST: Matches the platform the team already runs' --option 'gRPC: Adds streaming, see the note'; dispatch doc-read --issue HEAD-1 --artifact spec.md
proof.observed: the REST line reads the new description and the gRPC item is unchanged: '- gRPC: **Adds** streaming, see [the note](https://example.com/grpc)' with its second paragraph and its '- only if the client team agrees' sub-list still under it. The Go test TestAskOptionsEditKeepsWhatItDoesNotWrite asserts the same item node satisfies EqualWithBlockIDs against the node before the edit, so the block ids and the marks are the same node and not an equal rendering.
proof.negativeControl: the same three commands against a server built from 2b427f93 (port 8778, project MAIN): dispatch doc-read showed the ask flattened to '- gRPC: Adds streaming, see the note', the bold, the link's address, the second paragraph and the sub-list all deleted.

proof.command: dispatch edit-ask --ask 37e728a3-4763-4b66-8863-f67d49fbc32a --option 'REST: Matches the platform the team already runs' --option 'gRPC: Adds streaming'; dispatch doc-read --issue PROOF-2 --artifact spec.md
proof.observed: the gRPC item's first line reads the new plain 'gRPC: Adds streaming' while its second paragraph and its sub-list are still under it, unchanged. The Go test TestAskOptionsEditRewritesAnOptionAndKeepsTheRest asserts item.Children[1:] satisfy EqualWithBlockIDs against the original nodes.
proof.negativeControl:
dispatch edit-ask on the same ask sending REST alone, which would drop the gRPC item: refused 'options: the edit drops the option "gRPC", whose list item holds more than its plain line ... its item reads "- gRPC: **Adds** streaming, see [the note](https://example.com/grpc)

  A second paragraph the reviewer wrote under gRPC.

  - only if the client team agrees"; send that option back with this edit, or remove what the item holds with a document edit first (dispatch doc-edit, deleting a block by its id)', and dispatch doc-read showed the document unchanged.

A decision whose question a person emptied cannot be made from the CLI by a document edit (that edit is refused), but an upload of a new version of spec.md whose question paragraph holds only   makes exactly that state while the ask row stays open. That is how both proofs produced the precondition.

The merged option list is parsed on a budget of its own, not the caller write's. Measured: a preserved sub-list weighing 62,042 elements, under the 65,536 one write may make, was refused on a budget a 5,000-element question had charged first, and read with no refusal on a budget of its own (/legion/scratch/tmp/evidence/budget-measurement.txt).

api's TestIssueRanksStayOrderedPastLowercaseDigitsAndProductionShapedMoves refuses this pod's Postgres, whose default collation is byte order, and says so itself. It is the environment, not a failure.
deviations: Plan v1's design D3 cannot be built, and the plan's spec departure 1 is wrong. No document edit can write a paragraph inside an ask block: ApplyOps's insert finds its anchor through pmdoc.BlockBoundary, and documentBlock (packages/envoy/internal/dispatch/pmdoc/splice.go:72) loops over doc.Children alone, so an insert anchored on a block inside an ask lands beside the ask. A probe on the live service confirmed it, and `dispatch doc-edit` replacing a question with a space is refused 'ask block "..." has an empty question'. So a doc-edit that writes a question back is not a path today, and the one document edit of deletes plus the question that D3 names cannot be made.

What was built instead, which the INFRA-138 architect accepted at 2026-10-29T21:00Z: the ask edit itself writes the question into such a block, keeping every bullet list of the block in place whatever the content rule says, and the refusals name only the step that applies now. For a decision that is both empty-questioned and rule-breaking the path is three steps, each driven by the real command in A4, A5 and A6: the ask edit with a question, then the delete list the next refusal names, then the ask edit. No gate was relaxed and no edit operation was added.

A5's second row therefore reads the empty-question sentence and names no delete list, since a delete alone is refused while the question is empty; A6 follows the three steps in place of one document edit.

An options edit of a leniently read block holding more than one bullet list is refused with field options ('this decision holds more than one bullet list, so an options edit cannot say which list an option is in; send the question alone, and edit the options once the decision reads as one'), because the merge pairs options with the items of one list and such a block gives it no way to say which.

Settlement's restore of a decided ask's recorded wording (writeDecidedWording) drops a list item no decided option matches, whatever it holds, where the ask-edit route refuses. The refusal has no caller there, so refusing would leave the block and its row disagreeing for good and log the same refusal at every settlement of that document. TestRestoringADecidedWordingDropsAnOptionTheDecisionNeverHeld pins it, and TestAskOptionsEditRestoringADecidedWordingKeepsASubList pins that the restore keeps what a matched option holds.
openQuestions: None blocking. The simplify pass's three skipped findings are recorded in the pull request's Thermo line rather than here.
discoveredComplexity: The corpus follows had to repair every nested decision readAskBlockStrictly refuses, not only those pmdoc.AskContentError refuses: a nested decision of empty paragraphs keeps the content rule but asks nothing, and now has a path of its own, so the follow repairs it before the decision holding it, as the nested corpus already did for rule-breaking ones.

The refusal's delete list may now name a decision block, which the CLI's refuseRemovingOpenDecisionBlocks refuses while that decision's ask is open. A decision that never held a question never had a row, so the common case passes that guard; the refusal carries a clause for the case where a person emptied a decision that had one.
